rules.surface_condition: Cuts that split a name from an immediately following parenthetical/acronym (common in "Name (ACRONYM)" patterns) are over-valued by the prompt; penalize them.
rules.blamed_rule: Left or right stretch that ends or begins with a lexical token translators typically render reliably will tend to raise the measured value. Examples of such surface forms: numerals and formatted numbers (e.g., "1,200", "2050"), explicit dates, percentages, currency figures, and short fixed named phrases (e.g., organization names, place names). (Prediction to test: cuts adjacent to numerals/dates often score high.)
rules.proposed_rule: If the token immediately AFTER the marker is a parenthetical/acronym token (common short organization/abbrev tokens such as ISIL, MINAE, NSA, etc.), place the position into a lower target band (e.g. 10–40) instead of applying the usual 'name'-boost. This avoids cutting between an entity and its parenthetical identifier.

rules.surface_condition: Cuts immediately AFTER a numeral token (years, counts, small cardinals) are frequently over-valued by the prompt's numeral boost; reduce that boost.
rules.blamed_rule: Is the token immediately before the marker a numeral/date/percentage/name? If yes, bias score upward.
rules.proposed_rule: If the token immediately BEFORE the marker is NUM, do NOT apply a strong top-band boost; instead assign the position to a moderated target band (e.g. 10–60). In other words, treat numerals as context-dependent: keep a modest upward bias but suppress placements into the very top band when only a bare numeral anchors one side.

rules.surface_condition: Cuts where the token immediately AFTER the marker is a verb-form that commonly continues the clause (participles and short past participles: causing, reaching, named, released, etc.) are often over-scored when the comma/adjunct heuristic boosts them.
rules.blamed_rule: A marker that falls where a comma or parenthetical comma surrounds a self-contained adjunct (e.g., "yesterday,", "on Tuesday,", "as sources said,") often yields high scores if both sides can be translated faithfully by themselves. (Prediction to test: cuts after a comma that closes an embedded adjunct can score high.)
rules.proposed_rule: If the token immediately AFTER the marker is a participial/predicative verb form (common surface forms: tokens ending in 'ing' or a small enumerated list of frequent past-participles like 'named','released','reaching','causing'), reduce the comma/adjunct upward boost and place the cut in a lower band (e.g. 10–50). This treats commas followed by continuing predicates as less likely to mark independent adjunct boundaries.

tie_fix: Many heuristics apply identical discrete boosts (e.g. 'name' boost, 'numeral' boost, 'comma adjunct' boost) so after rounding several markers receive the same numeric value; add a tiny deterministic position-dependent offset (e.g. epsilon × marker_index) before integerizing to avoid ties.
summary: The prompt systematically over-weights surface anchors (names, numerals, comma-adjunct heuristics), causing it to favor cuts that split entities from parentheticals, split bare numerals from their context, or split before continuing participial clauses — even when the remainder contradicts or fragments the segment. Apply targeted down-ranks: (1) avoid cutting between a name and its parenthetical acronym; (2) suppress aggressive top-band boosts for bare numerals; (3) suppress comma-driven boosts when the next token is a continuing participial/predicative verb. These changes focus the model away from brittle surface shortcuts that produce contradiction/fragment errors.
